AD.ACCOUNT.STALE_ENABLED.title: Accounts nobody uses are still switched on
AD.ACCOUNT.STALE_ENABLED.whyItMatters: Every enabled account is a door into the network. Accounts belonging to people who left, or service accounts nobody maintains any more, are rarely monitored and their passwords are rarely changed, so an attacker who guesses or steals one is unlikely to be noticed.
whatToDo: Confirm with the account owner or their manager whether each account is still needed.
Disable the accounts that are no longer needed, and move them to a dedicated organizational unit so they are easy to review later.
Delete them after a retention period that suits your organization, typically 30 to 90 days after disabling.
For service accounts that must stay, document the owner and set a password rotation schedule.

references.label: Microsoft: Active Directory Domain Services documentation

AD.POLICY.WEAK_PASSWORD.title: The domain password rules are easy to defeat
AD.POLICY.WEAK_PASSWORD.whyItMatters: The domain password policy sets the floor for every account in the domain. Short passwords can be cracked offline in a short time once an attacker obtains a password hash, and with no lockout threshold an attacker can keep guessing passwords over the network without ever being locked out.
whatToDo: Raise the minimum password length to at least 14 characters in the Default Domain Policy.
Turn password complexity back on, or replace it with a longer minimum length plus a banned password list.
Set an account lockout threshold so repeated failed sign-ins are stopped, and pair it with a lockout duration your help desk can live with.
Test the change on a small group first, because raising these settings affects every user at their next password change.

references.label: Microsoft: Active Directory Domain Services documentation

AD.PRIVILEGE.EXCESSIVE_ADMIN_MEMBERSHIP.title: Too many people have full control of the domain
AD.PRIVILEGE.EXCESSIVE_ADMIN_MEMBERSHIP.whyItMatters: Members of Domain Admins can do anything in the domain, including reading every password hash. Each extra member is another account an attacker can target to take over the whole environment, and nested groups make this worse because the real member count is larger than the group appears to hold.
whatToDo: List everyone who is currently a member, including members inherited through nested groups, and confirm each one still needs that level of access.
Remove day to day user accounts from privileged groups. Give administrators a separate admin account used only for administrative work.
Avoid nesting ordinary groups such as help desk groups inside privileged groups, because it hides the true membership.
Review the membership on a fixed schedule, for example once a quarter.

references.label: Detecting and mitigating Active Directory compromises (joint advisory)

AD.PRIVILEGE.UNCONSTRAINED_DELEGATION.title: Some machines and accounts can impersonate any user who connects to them
AD.PRIVILEGE.UNCONSTRAINED_DELEGATION.whyItMatters: A machine or account trusted for unconstrained delegation keeps a reusable copy of the Kerberos ticket of everyone who connects to it. If an attacker controls it and a domain administrator has signed in there, the attacker can replay that ticket and take over the domain. Nothing has to be exploited for this to be true: it is what the setting does. It can be set on a computer, on an ordinary account running a service, or on a managed service account, and the Account category column below says which kind each one is, because the fix differs.
whatToDo: Find out what the service actually does before changing anything. Delegation is switched on so that a service can pass a user's identity on to a second service, for example a web application reaching a database as the person using it. Turning it off will break that, so confirm what depends on it first and plan the change with whoever owns the service.

Prefer narrowing it to constrained delegation over removing it outright. Constrained delegation lets the account act for a user against a named list of services and nothing else, which usually keeps the application working while closing the exposure.

For a computer account, or an ordinary user or service account: open the account in Active Directory Users and Computers and go to the Delegation tab. Choose “Trust this computer for delegation to specified services only” and list those services, or “Do not trust this computer for delegation” if it turns out none are needed. On a user account the tab only appears once the account has a service name registered.

For a managed service account or a group managed service account there is no Delegation tab, so use PowerShell. To remove it: Set-ADAccountControl -Identity 'name$' -TrustedForDelegation $false. To move to constrained delegation instead: Set-ADServiceAccount -Identity 'name$' -Add @{'msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo' = 'CIFS/server.example.com'}. Remember the trailing dollar sign in the name.

Protect your administrators separately, so that a machine like this cannot replay their tickets even while it is being fixed. Add them to the Protected Users group, or tick “Account is sensitive and cannot be delegated” on each administrative account.
Until it is resolved, treat each of these as being as trusted as the most privileged person who signs in to it, and keep administrators off them.

references.label: Joint advisory: Detecting and mitigating Active Directory compromises
Microsoft: Configure Kerberos delegation for group managed service accounts

AD.PRIVILEGE.KERBEROASTING.title: Service accounts whose passwords can be cracked offline
AD.PRIVILEGE.KERBEROASTING.whyItMatters: These accounts run services, so they are registered in the directory under a service name. Active Directory is designed to hand any signed-in user a ticket for a registered service, and that ticket is locked with the service account's own password. An attacker with any ordinary account, even a brand new one, can therefore collect those tickets and then try to guess the passwords on their own computer, where no lockout stops them and nothing in your logs looks unusual. The whole attack needs no special permission at all. If one of these accounts is also an administrator, cracking its password hands over the entire domain.
whatToDo: Give each of these accounts a long random password, 25 characters or more. Length is what defeats offline guessing, and nobody has to type a service account password by hand.
Remove any of these accounts from Domain Admins and other administrative groups. A service almost never needs domain-wide rights, and those are the accounts worth the attacker's time.

Set the account to use AES encryption only, by ticking the two AES options under the account's Delegation or Account tab. Accounts left on the default still accept the older RC4 encryption, which is far quicker to crack.
Where the service supports it, replace the account with a group managed service account. The directory then generates and rotates the password itself and this problem goes away.
Remove the service name registration from any account that no longer runs a service.

references.label: Joint advisory: Detecting and mitigating Active Directory compromises
Microsoft: Group managed service accounts overview

AD.POLICY.RISKY_GPO.title: Group policy is handing out passwords or privileges it should not
AD.POLICY.RISKY_GPO.whyItMatters: Group policy is stored as ordinary files on a share that every computer in the domain has to read, which means every person in the domain can read it too. Three things found there are worth acting on. A password saved by a group policy preference is scrambled with a key Microsoft published years ago, so anyone who can open the file can read the password. A powerful Windows privilege handed to a group that is far broader than it should be gives that power to everyone in the group, on every machine the policy reaches, and several of those privileges let an ordinary account take over the machine. And a policy that switches the guest account on opens a way in that needs no account at all. The Issue column below says which of the three each row is, and the Detail column says exactly who was granted what.
whatToDo: For a stored password, treat it as already known. Change the password on every account it was set for, then delete the preference that set it. Finding and removing the file is not enough on its own, because anyone who copied it still has the password.

Where the Issue column says the format was not recognised, the tool found a cpassword attribute but its value did not look like the scrambled form, so it may be a placeholder or a damaged entry rather than a recoverable password. Treat it as a question rather than an emergency: find out what wrote it, and remove the attribute either way, because nothing should be writing passwords into these files at all.

Replace that preference with something that does not store a secret. Local Administrator Password Solution manages local administrator passwords without putting them in a file, and a scheduled task or service can run as a managed service account instead of a named account with a password.

For a dangerous privilege, read the Detail column to see who it was granted to. Authenticated Users, Domain Users and Everyone each mean every account in the domain. Anonymous Logon means no account at all, and the guest groups mean guest access, which is a smaller set of people but not a more trusted one.
Then find out which application asked for the privilege. These are usually added for one piece of software and then left in a policy that applies far more widely than intended.
Narrow it. Grant the privilege to a specific group containing only the accounts that need it, and link the policy only to the machines that run that software, rather than to the whole domain.
For the guest account, set the policy to disable it unless you have a documented reason to keep it, and check whether anything is relying on it before you change it.
Check the scope of each policy before changing it. This report reads what a policy says, not where it currently applies, so confirm in Group Policy Management which machines it reaches.

references.label: Microsoft MS14-025: Vulnerability in Group Policy Preferences
Joint advisory: Detecting and mitigating Active Directory compromises

AD.TRUST.RISKY_TRUST.technicalName: Risky domain or forest trust configuration
AD.TRUST.RISKY_TRUST.title: A trust with another organization lets it reach further in than it should
AD.TRUST.RISKY_TRUST.whyItMatters: A trust is a decision to accept sign-ins from a directory you do not run. That is often necessary and is not a problem by itself. What matters is how far the other side can reach once it is trusted, and that is decided by a few settings that are easy to get wrong and invisible unless somebody looks. The most serious is SID filtering. With it in place, your domain controller throws away any claim of group membership that arrives from the other side. Without it, whoever runs the trusted domain can simply assert that they belong to your Domain Admins group and be believed. They do not have to break into anything here. The Issue column below says which setting each row is about, and the Detail column says what it means in practice. The rest are smaller: a forest trust marked to be treated as external lowers the filtering across the whole boundary, ticket delegation left open across a forest trust is what lets a delegation problem on either side reach the other, RC4 is far weaker than the encryption available, and selective authentication left off means accounts from the other side are treated as ordinary authenticated users here instead of being allowed only on the servers you nominate.
whatToDo: Start with the trust itself rather than the setting. Find out who asked for it, what still depends on it, and whether the relationship is current. A trust nobody can account for should be removed, not repaired.
For SID filtering, remember that the other side's security is now your security. Before you decide this is acceptable, ask how that domain is administered and who there could abuse it.

Turn filtering on with netdom trust, using /quarantine:yes for an external trust or /enablesidhistory:no for a forest trust. Test it first: if anybody was migrated between the two domains and still relies on their old identity, turning filtering on will break their access, which is the usual reason it was turned off.
If a forest trust is marked to be treated as external, find out whether the migration that caused it ever finished. If it did, remove the attribute.

Block ticket delegation across a forest trust unless something specifically needs it, and read the unconstrained delegation finding alongside this one, because the two together are what make a cross-forest attack possible.
Move the trust off RC4 once both sides support AES, and test it outside business hours, because a mismatch here stops authentication across the trust entirely.
Turn selective authentication on where the other side only needs a small number of your servers, then grant the Allowed to Authenticate right on exactly those servers.

Check the direction yourself. This tool records whether each trust is inbound, outbound or both, but it does not judge it, because which direction exposes you depends on how the trust was created and on what the other side's administrators can do, and a scan from here cannot see either.

references.label: Microsoft: Securing domain and forest trusts
Microsoft: When to create an external trust, including SID filter quarantining and the netdom syntax
Joint advisory: Detecting and mitigating Active Directory compromises

AD.ACCOUNT.LAPS_MISSING.technicalName: Local administrator passwords not managed by LAPS
AD.ACCOUNT.LAPS_MISSING.title: The local administrator password on these computers is not being changed automatically
AD.ACCOUNT.LAPS_MISSING.whyItMatters: Every Windows computer has a built-in local administrator account. It is not a domain account, so the domain password policy does not touch it, and nothing makes it change on its own. When those passwords are set from an image, a build script, or a technician doing the same thing on every machine, they end up identical across the whole estate. One of them, read from one machine, is then a working administrator password on every machine. That is the ordinary way a single infected laptop becomes the whole network, and it needs no software flaw: the password simply works where it is tried next. LAPS is the tool that fixes this. It sets a different random password on each computer and rotates it on a schedule, so a password taken from one machine is worth nothing anywhere else. The Issue column below says which situation each computer is in. Not managed by LAPS means it has never been covered. Overdue for rotation means it was covered and has stopped, so the password sitting on it now is as old as the date shown. This finding reports that the control is missing. It cannot tell you whether those passwords actually are the same, which is a thing you confirm by hand.
whatToDo: If the finding says LAPS is not installed in this domain at all, this is a project rather than a fix. Windows LAPS is built into current versions of Windows and Windows Server, so on a reasonably current estate there is usually nothing to install on the clients: the schema extension plus a Group Policy setting is the whole job.
Extend the schema with Update-LapsADSchema. This is a one-way change and needs Schema Admins, so do it deliberately, with a backup, and not for the first time on a production domain.

Decide who is allowed to read the passwords before you turn it on, and grant it with Set-LapsADReadPasswordPermission. Getting this wrong in the generous direction hands every helpdesk account a local administrator password for every machine, which trades one problem for another.
Grant the computers permission to write their own password with Set-LapsADComputerSelfPermission, scoped to the organizational units that hold them.

Turn it on by policy, under Computer Configuration, Administrative Templates, System, LAPS. Set the password to be backed up to Active Directory, and set a rotation age. Thirty days is the common choice.

For the computers listed as not managed, the usual cause is that the policy does not reach the organizational unit they sit in. Check where each one actually is in the directory before assuming the agent is broken.

For the computers listed as overdue, the password is still valid and still in place, so this is not harmless. Check whether the machine is still switched on and talking to the domain, and whether the policy that was managing it was changed or unlinked. A machine that has not been seen for months may simply be gone, in which case remove the computer account.
Do not treat this as finished once LAPS is deployed. Consider also disabling the built-in local administrator account where nothing needs it, so there is no password to manage in the first place.

references.label: Microsoft: Overview of Windows LAPS PowerShell cmdlets
Microsoft: Windows LAPS schema extensions reference
Joint advisory: Detecting and mitigating Active Directory compromises
